title: Choose the visual world for SMTPMonster
question: The roll assigned The Sorting Case. Keep it, take an alternate, or re-roll.

options.label: The Sorting Case
options.lineage: Post-office letter sorting cases: steel pigeonholes with brass label holders
options.thesis: A wall of pigeonholes, one per recipient, and every letter ends up in exactly one box: yours.
options.viewport: The page IS the sorting case: a grid of labelled slots (customer@, ceo@, billing@...) fills the right two-thirds; the sign-up field is the blank card in the one open label holder, and letters addressed to everyone else slide into it.
options.risk: If the slots read as a feature-card grid, it collapses into the template; the case must stay one object.

raised.raise: Hierarchy by scale contrast alone: one huge headline against tiny typed labels, no badges or icon tiles.
States stamp, never vanish: a rerouted letter keeps its original address struck through with the new one stamped beside it.
Depth only by overlap: cards, tags and slots stack flat, no drop shadows or glows anywhere.
Three values per region and every rule drawn at one pixel.

options.label: Return to Sender
options.lineage: Undeliverable-mail forwarding labels and rubber stamps
options.thesis: Every email your app sends comes back wearing the yellow ‘Return to Sender’ sticker.
options.viewport: One giant kraft envelope addressed to a customer, overprinted with the yellow label that redirects it to your address; the label's address line is the sign-up field.
options.risk: The postal-envelope metaphor is the most literal reading of email; plenty of mail tools reach for it.

options.label: Departures Board
options.thesis: Your app's outbound mail as a departures board where every destination flips to your inbox.
options.viewport: A full-width board of outbound messages; the TO column cascades character by character from customer addresses to yours, and the sign-up field is the board's destination row.
options.case: Strong product clarity (the reroute is literally visible) but split-flap is a well-worn dev-tool trope, so it loses on audience identification.
options.risk: Reads as a retro novelty if the board is not strictly ruled.

options.label: Ticket Wallet
options.thesis: Each message as a coupon stamped VOID and reissued to you.
options.viewport: A coupon book of messages, each one stamped rerouted.
options.case: Travel is foreign to an SMTP relay; loses on both axes.
options.kept: States stamp themselves; nothing disappears, it reroutes.

options.label: Type Specimen
options.thesis: A live specimen where an axis slider morphs the page.
options.viewport: One giant glyph and a slider.
options.case: No link to mail or development safety; loses both axes.
options.risk: Pure type showcase with no product.

options.label: Layered Papercut
options.thesis: A symmetrical roundel built up from flat cut layers.
options.viewport: A layered roundel with the product inside.
options.case: Folk craft has nothing to say to a developer configuring SMTP.
options.kept: Depth by overlap only, never by shading.

options.label: Centre-rail Reference
options.thesis: Two columns twinned around a rail of keys.
options.viewport: A small dense text block in a wide margin.
options.case: Too scholarly for a one-field sign-up page.
options.kept: Three values only; every rule at one pixel.

options.label: Cloud Quarry
options.case: No truthful mapping to an SMTP loopback.
options.kept: Stacked blocks with clear gaps between sections.

canonCard.label: The category standard
canonCard.thesis: A clean developer-tool landing page, executed impeccably.
canonCard.viewport: Headline and email field on the left, a code snippet and inbox screenshot on the right.
canonCard.risk: Indistinguishable from every other dev tool by design.
